members.title: UK unemployment unexpectedly eases to 4.6%, as government prepares to release Milburn report
members.lead: Wage growth falls to to 3.5% in September, as ministers examine how best to get young people into work Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on young people Who are the Neets? UK youth job crisis in five charts The UK unemployment rate has unexpectedly fallen as the government prepares to release a major report on the youth jobs crisis. The unemployment rate was 4.6% in September, dipping from 4.7% in August, according to the Office for National Statistics. City economists had expected it to remain at 4.7%. Continue reading...

members.title: Youth unemployment plan could cut welfare bill before election, says Milburn, but overall savings will take years – UK politics live
members.lead: Alan Milburn says his plan could cut the welfare bill before the next election, but overall savings will take years Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on ‘new deal’ for young people This is what the opposition parties have been saying about the Alan Milburn proposals. The full report has not formally been published yet, but it has been circulating in Westminster on an embargoed basis since yesterday and so the parties all know what it says. The Conservatives says Milburn should be cutting welfare more aggressively. This is from Helen Whately, the shadow work and pensions secretary. Conservatives agree with Alan Milburn on the problem, and we want his review to succeed. Where Milburn gets it right, we’ll back him. Especially where he adopts our proposals like shifting from cash sickness benefits to support for milder conditions and cutting national insurance for young people. Alan Milburn is right to criticise the tax and regulation burdens Labour have imposed on businesses. But his review is too cautious on reversing that damage and too often his answer is the big and expensive hand of the state. Overall, it fails to bring down the welfare bill, proposes billions more in government spending and won’t make the slightest difference for young people stuck on welfare now - because nothing will happen for at least three years. Successive governments have allowed a generation to fall through the cracks. Nearly a million young people are now out of work or training, which is more than there are job vacancies in the entire country. ‘Work not welfare’ means nothing when the work simply isn’t there. If ministers want to halve the number of Neets by 2036, they need a plan for growth. That means scrapping Labour’s jobs tax, joining the EU single market and cutting the cost of doing business, so firms can afford to hire young people again.
